objectives.name: Mirror Match
objectives.goal: Make an invertible, non-diagonal symmetric matrix: Aᵀ = A and det(A) ≠ 0.
objectives.check: Aᵀ = A, det(A) = −1, and off-diagonal entries are nonzero.
objectives.note: Transpose alone does not turn an asymmetric matrix into a symmetric one. A suitable interchange or red-card correction can finish this goal.

objectives.name: Signed Identity +
objectives.check: This is I₃ and wins the +1 variant. Negating it wins the −1 variant.
objectives.note: LU can finish the +1 variant from an upper triangular matrix by choosing L = I. Dimension changes may make a smaller identity easier to construct; generation tests must include those routes.

objectives.name: Signed Identity -
objectives.check: This is -I₃ and wins the -1 variant.
objectives.note: LU can finish the +1 variant from an upper triangular matrix by choosing L = I. Dimension changes may make a smaller identity easier to construct; generation tests must include those routes.

objectives.name: Diagonal Diversity
objectives.goal: Make a diagonal matrix with every diagonal entry nonzero and at least three distinct diagonal values.
objectives.check: The diagonal values 1, 2, and 3 are nonzero and distinct.
objectives.note: A 2×2 matrix cannot qualify. For an invertible lower triangular A with the required diagonal values, choosing U from LU can finish the goal.

objectives.name: Two-way Balance
objectives.goal: Make every row sum and every column sum exactly 1, with at least one negative entry.
objectives.check: All three row sums and column sums are 1; negative entries occur.
objectives.note: Row sums and column sums both equal to 1 force a square shape: their totals are m and n. Size 2 is excluded here because its negative-entry solutions automatically satisfy Mirror Match, reducing variety.

objectives.name: Opposite Reflection
objectives.goal: Make a nonzero skew-symmetric matrix: Aᵀ = −A.
objectives.check: The diagonal is zero and opposite entries have opposite signs; A is nonzero.
objectives.note: A real skew-symmetric matrix of odd size is singular; even sizes may be invertible. A single interchange can finish some specially arranged matrices, so check actual opening hands rather than assuming uniform difficulty.

objectives.name: Return to Start
objectives.goal: Make a non-diagonal matrix with A² = Iₙ.
objectives.check: A² = I₃; the off-diagonal 1 makes A non-diagonal.
objectives.note: From I, swapping two rows or two columns produces a valid non-diagonal involution. Non-diagonal is required, so diagonal sign patterns and ±I alone do not win.

objectives.name: Volume-Preserving Mix
objectives.goal: Make det(A) = 1, with at least two nonzero entries in every row and every column.
objectives.check: det(A) = 1; each row and column contains at least two nonzero entries.
objectives.note: LU no longer gives an automatic win: L has only one nonzero entry in its first row, and U has at most one in its last row. Fixed printed constants also remove arbitrary determinant tuning.

objectives.name: Projection
objectives.goal: Make a non-diagonal rank-2 matrix satisfying A² = A.
objectives.check: A² = A and rank(A) = 2; A is non-diagonal.
objectives.note: A 2×2 rank-2 idempotent must be I₂ and therefore cannot qualify. Low-rank red cards provide useful ingredients, but making a matrix singular alone is insufficient.

objectives.name: Three-step Collapse
objectives.check: A² has a 1 in position (1,3), while A³ is the zero matrix.
objectives.note: Size 2 cannot have nilpotency index 3. Zero matrices and rank-1 shortcuts do not qualify. Check powers exactly rather than treating a zero determinant as sufficient.

objectives.name: Three-step Return
objectives.goal: Make A³ = Iₙ, with A not a signed permutation matrix. A signed permutation matrix has exactly one nonzero entry in every row and column, and those entries are ±1.
objectives.check: A³ = I₃; rows with two nonzero entries show that A is not a signed permutation matrix.
objectives.note: The exclusion prevents a simple three-cycle permutation from completing the goal. Over real matrices, triangular LU outputs cannot produce a nontrivial order-3 solution.

objectives.name: Orthogonal Columns
objectives.goal: Make a tall matrix whose columns are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, with no zero rows. Equivalently, AᵀA is diagonal with positive diagonal entries.
objectives.check: AᵀA = diag(3,2), and every row is nonzero.
objectives.note: The columns need not have unit length, so integer solutions are possible. Appending a row r adds rᵀr to AᵀA; it changes orthogonality rather than guaranteeing it. This goal is the transpose counterpart of C12.

objectives.name: Orthogonal Rows
objectives.goal: Make a wide matrix whose rows are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, with no zero columns. Equivalently, AAᵀ is diagonal with positive diagonal entries.
objectives.check: AAᵀ = diag(3,2), and every column is nonzero.
objectives.note: Transpose converts a completed C11 matrix into a C12 matrix. Appending a column can alter row dot products, providing a reason to change dimensions rather than merely adding empty space.

objectives.name: Rectangular Balance
objectives.goal: For an m×n matrix with m ≠ n, make every row sum n and every column sum m, with at least one negative entry.
objectives.check: Here m = 2 and n = 3: each row sums to 3 and each column sums to 2; negative entries occur.
objectives.note: These totals agree at mn, so rectangular solutions are possible. The negative-entry requirement excludes the all-ones matrix. Appending changes both the shape and the required row or column sums; check the complete result again.

objectives.name: Zero-sum Orthogonal Rows
objectives.goal: Make a wide matrix with nonzero pairwise orthogonal rows, every row sum 0, and no zero columns. Equivalently, A1ₙ = 0 and AAᵀ is diagonal with positive diagonal entries, where 1ₙ is the column vector of n ones.
objectives.check: Both row sums are 0, their dot product is 0, and AAᵀ = diag(2,6). No column is zero.
objectives.note: This intentionally strengthens C12 by putting the all-ones vector in the nullspace. Wide shape is necessary: independent zero-sum rows lie in an (n−1)-dimensional subspace.
